historyTimeline.h2: Ford Puma 1.0 EcoBoost Mild Hybrid - Engine History & Specs at a Glance
historyTimeline.intro: When the 1.0 EcoBoost Mild Hybrid variant launched, it served as the efficient, electrified flagship of the modern Ford Puma range, introducing a 48V belt-integrated starter generator (BISG) to improve fuel economy and refine stop-start operation.

milestones.description: B7JA / B7JB introduced, 1.0L EcoBoost mHEV, 125 PS (92 kW), featuring a timing chain for the camshafts but retaining a belt-in-oil drive for the oil pump to meet stricter emissions standards.
B7JC introduced for the Puma ST-Line, offering 155 PS (114 kW) with the same mHEV architecture, updated thermal management, and sportier tuning.
B7JE introduced for automatic transmission variants, maintaining the 125 PS output while integrating seamlessly with the 7-speed dual-clutch transmission.

historyTimeline.closingNote: Every engine fitted to the Ford Puma 1.0 EcoBoost Mild Hybrid is covered below, with UK rebuilt pricing and known failure points.

problems.h4: Oil Pump Wet Belt Degradation - Why the Ford Puma 1.0 EcoBoost Mild Hybrid (B7JA/B7JB/B7JC/B7JE) Suffers Oil Starvation
problems.affectedModels: Ford Puma 1.0 EcoBoost Mild Hybrid (B7JA, B7JB, B7JC, B7JE, 2019-present)
problems.rootCause: While the camshafts are driven by a timing chain, the oil pump is driven by a belt running submerged in the engine oil. If the incorrect oil specification (must be Ford WSS-M2C948-B 0W-20) is used, or service intervals are extended, the belt degrades, sheds rubber debris, and blocks the oil pickup strainer, causing catastrophic oil starvation and bottom-end failure.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Drop sump, replace oil pump belt, clean oil pickup strainer, refill with correct spec oil
repairOptions.longevity: Highly recommended preventative maintenance at 80k miles or 8 years

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Supply & fit, upgraded components addressing the original failure point, 12-month warranty
repairOptions.longevity: The right call if oil starvation has already caused bottom-end or turbocharger damage

Replacement cost is typically small relative to vehicle value, making a full rebuilt engine a highly justifiable expense to preserve the vehicle's substantial market value.
problems.recommendation: Preventative oil pump belt replacement is strongly recommended at 80,000 miles or 8 years. If oil starvation has already caused bottom-end knocking or turbocharger damage, a full rebuilt engine is the only reliable long-term solution, as a standalone oil pump repair will not reverse existing internal scoring.

items.question: Does the Ford Puma 1.0 EcoBoost Mild Hybrid have a wet belt?
items.answer: While the camshafts are driven by a timing chain, the Ford Puma 1.0 EcoBoost Mild Hybrid still uses a "wet belt" (belt-in-oil) to drive the oil pump.

Debris from a failing belt can block the oil pickup strainer, causing catastrophic engine seizure.

items.question: What is the difference between the B7JA and B7JC Ford Puma 1.0 EcoBoost Mild Hybrid engines?
items.answer: The primary difference between the B7JA and B7JC codes fitted to the Ford Puma 1.0 EcoBoost Mild Hybrid is the power output and associated trim levels.
keyPoints: The B7JA produces 125 PS (92 kW) and is typically fitted to Zetec and Titanium trims.
The B7JC produces 155 PS (114 kW) and is exclusively fitted to higher-spec ST-Line X and ST-Line Vignale trims.
Mechanically, they share the same core mHEV architecture, but the B7JC features a larger turbocharger and different ECU mapping.
